items.title: Wait for pull request events with GitHub CLI
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub CLI now supports GitHub Event Streams. With gh v2.105.0, you and your agents can wait for a pull request to change with a single command instead of polling it in a loop. Run gh event listen with a pull request URL and the events you care about, such as a submitted review. It creates the subscription, opens the stream and prints each event as a line of JSON. By default, it exits after the first event, so it slots into scripts and agent loops. Use --count to wait for several events, --follow to keep listening, and --timeout to stop waiting. Use --jq or --template to pull out just the fields you need. You can wait for submitted reviews, pull request state and head changes, merge conflicts and completed check suites. To manage subscriptions directly, use gh event subscription create, list, view, and delete. Agents discover the new commands on their own: gh pr create, gh pr view, gh run view, gh run watch, and gh api now suggest gh event listen instead of polling. Availability The gh event commands are in preview and may change. They require access to Event Streams, which is in preview on GitHub.com. To get access, sign up for the Event Streams waitlist. To get started, upgrade to gh v2.105.0 or later. For details, see the gh event manual and the Event Streams documentation, or run gh event --help. Share your feedback in the GitHub Community discussion. The post Wait for pull request events with GitHub CLI appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: gh event listen lets agents and scripts wait for PR events such as reviews without polling, which helps our agent loops and gated review pipelines.

items.title: Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Enterprise Live Migrations (ELM) from Azure DevOps Services to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency is now generally available. You can move your repositories while your teams keep working, then cut over on your schedule. Manage migrations through the portal or CLI: Choose a guided experience in the Azure DevOps portal or script your migrations with the Azure DevOps CLI. Pre-migration validation and lifecycle tracking help you identify issues and monitor progress before cutover. Cut over on your schedule: ELM continuously syncs changes from Azure DevOps to GitHub, so developers can keep contributing throughout the migration. When you’re ready, complete the move with a brief cutover at a time that works for your teams. Bring your development history with you: ELM syncs Git history, branches, tags, and pull requests, including titles, descriptions, comments, and user history. Your Azure DevOps branch policies migrate as GitHub branch rulesets. Keep using Azure Boards and Azure Pipelines: You can have ELM create the Azure Boards connection and rewire Azure Pipelines to your migrated GitHub repository, reducing manual setup after cutover. Your work items and pipeline definitions stay in Azure DevOps. Ready to start your migration journey? Visit Microsoft’s ELM documentation to learn more and get started. The post Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Live migrations from Azure DevOps to GitHub Enterprise are now generally available. This only matters to the occasional enterprise client moving off Azure DevOps.

items.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux runner images now generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9 and RHEL 10 images for GitHub-hosted larger runners are now generally available. Originally introduced in public preview in June 2026 in partnership with Red Hat, these images are now fully supported for production workflows in GitHub Actions. You can use RHEL images to run your workflows on the same operating system you deploy to, or as the foundation for custom images that include your required tools, dependencies, and configurations. To get started, create a new Linux x64 larger runner and choose your desired RHEL image under partner images. If you’ve been using RHEL images during the public preview, no action is required. Your existing runners and workflows will continue to work as-is. RHEL images are available for larger runners on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud plans. To learn more, see Managing larger runners and Using custom images. The post Red Hat Enterprise Linux runner images now generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.excerpt: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen, who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models, to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model, while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model. In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das, a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs. It includes com

items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.excerpt: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette (datasette install datasette-arrows) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette, projects

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.excerpt: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT(). Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql, postgresql, replication, scaling, wikipedia, ai-security-r
items.why_it_matters: PostgreSQL 19 is a major release of a core database in our stack and was delayed by a wave of vulnerability fixes. New features like WAIT FOR LSN read-your-writes consistency matter for Supabase and Postgres clients.

items.title: Scaling Linear's GTM to $100M+ ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: Over half the issues created in Linear now come from agents instead of people. I sat down with Cristina Cordova (COO at Linear) to talk about what that does to the software industry. They shipped an MCP server early, watched agents take over half the work, and then had to answer an uncomfortable question: if your product is mostly a database an agent writes to, why would humans open the app? A few things I didn't expect. Three weeks into the job she stood up at an offsite and crossed "go enterprise" off the company goals, and they didn't go after enterprise until two years later. They've never hired a single SDR, and they don't do forward deployed engineering. We also got into the AI budget every startup is tapping into and why she thinks it's already tightening, what it takes to cannibalize yourself before someone else does, and pricing on outcomes. items.why_it_matters: Linear says over half its issues now come from agents through its MCP server. That is a useful sign of how agent-driven workflows are changing SaaS products and how clients build them.
